All 100 simulations are used. The best design scores a **mean L/D of 117.05**, about 25% above NACA 4412 (93.5). None of the 100 designs failed.

**Best design:** `u = [0.28, 0.48, 0.57, 0.75, 0.43, 0.66, 0.67]`
- **Thickness weights:** a0 ≈ 0.57, a2 ≈ 0.91, a3 ≈ 1.11. Maximum thickness sits at about 41% of the chord, with a fairly sharp leading edge.
- **Camber weights:** b ≈ [0.20, 0.07, 0.16, 0.17], about 3.4% camber peaking near 56% of the chord. There's a dip at b1 and more camber towards the back (aft loading).

| CL | alpha (°) | cd | L/D | cm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.4 | −0.57 | 0.00518 | 77.2 | −0.114 |
| 0.6 | 1.50 | 0.00487 | 123.2 | −0.108 |
| 0.8 | 2.78 | 0.00531 | 150.7 | −0.122 |

**What I learned about the design space:**
- **Camber level mattered most.** Drag only stays low (the "drag bucket") over a range of lift coefficients. With little camber (about 1.5%), CL 0.8 falls outside that range and drag rises (cd about 0.009). With a lot (4.5%), CL 0.4 needs a negative angle of attack and drag rises there instead. About 3.4–3.5% kept all three targets at low drag.
- **The objective favours the CL 0.8 point.** Cutting drag by a given amount raises L/D at CL 0.8 about twice as much as at CL 0.4. So the best designs accept a little extra drag at CL 0.4 (cd about 0.0052) to get cd about 0.0053 at CL 0.8.
- **How the camber is spread matters about as much as how much there is.** Camber concentrated near the front lowered the score (about 105). Loading it towards the back helped CL 0.8 most. Adding camber right at the leading edge (b0 high) with a dip at b1 gave the last gains, likely because the airflow meets the leading edge more smoothly across the angle range.
- **Moving maximum thickness from 33% to about 40–42% of the chord helped.** It lowered drag at all three points, probably by keeping the boundary layer smooth (laminar) for longer. Beyond about 45% it got worse, and at 53% drag rose sharply at CL 0.6 and 0.8, which looks like the flow separating early.
- **The leading edge can't be too sharp.** a0 between roughly 0.25 and 0.4 (in u) worked well. At 0.1 the airfoil was close to stalling at CL 0.8 (cd 0.020). Too blunt (0.7) raised drag everywhere.
- **The trailing-edge wedge (a3) has a narrow sweet spot around 0.55–0.6.** Larger values helped CL 0.4 but hurt CL 0.8, and both extremes (0.2 and 0.9) were clearly worse.
- **Near the best, the landscape is flat and a little noisy.** Many neighbouring designs scored 115–117, and the last steps were about ±0.5. That is probably within the jitter of XFoil's transition prediction, so the exact top design may not be meaningfully better than its neighbours.
